title: UPI Said Pending
hook: A customer's bank shows the money debited, but your app says the order failed. They screenshot it, post it, and ten more people report the same thing.
context: Checkout flow integrated with a payment gateway and UPI, with an order service and an inventory service.
solution_brief: Treat timeouts as unknown, give every payment a stable identity, verify state through webhooks plus polling plus reconciliation, publish events through an outbox, and compensate with refunds when later steps fail. PENDING is a first-class state. Idempotency key per payment attempt. Webhook, status poller and settlement reconciliation. Transactional outbox for reliable events. Saga with idempotent compensating refund.

steps.prompt: Your code calls the payment gateway, the call times out after 10 seconds, and you mark the order FAILED. The gateway later confirms the payment succeeded. What was the design mistake?
steps.context_note: A timeout is not a failure. It is silence.

options.text: Treating a timeout as a failure rather than an unknown outcome
Using a 10-second timeout instead of a longer five-minute timeout
Not retrying the charge immediately after the timeout
Using a gateway that can time out at all

steps.explanation: After a timeout you do not know whether the other side processed the payment, so the order should wait in an explicit PENDING state until its status is confirmed. A longer timeout shrinks the uncertain window but never removes it, and an immediate retry could charge the customer twice.
steps.bottleneck_note: Distributed calls have three outcomes: success, failure and unknown. Model all three.

steps.prompt: The order is PENDING and the user taps Pay again. What lets the system avoid a second charge for the same order?
steps.context_note: Screens that spin invite a second tap.

options.text: Disabling the Pay button until the page is reloaded
A fresh random reference on every tap, so that each attempt can be tracked later
An error message that sends the user to support
A stable attempt ID used as an idempotency key, unique in your database

steps.explanation: A stable ID per logical payment makes repeated submissions collapse into one, and enforcing uniqueness in your own database as well as at the gateway covers both client double-taps and server retries. A new reference per tap creates a new charge each time, and disabling the button only guards one client.
steps.bottleneck_note: Every money-moving call needs a stable identity.

steps.prompt: PENDING orders must eventually become SUCCESS or FAILED. How do you resolve them reliably?
steps.context_note: A webhook is only a notification, and notifications get delayed, duplicated or lost.

options.text: Rely on webhooks alone, because the gateway retries any webhook that fails to arrive
Mark orders still PENDING after one minute as FAILED
Idempotent webhooks, a poller for old PENDING orders, and daily reconciliation

steps.explanation: Webhooks are an optimisation rather than a guarantee, so a poller catches the lost ones and settlement reconciliation is the final source of truth. Failing every order after a minute recreates the original bug of declaring failure on money that may have moved.
steps.bottleneck_note: Never trust a single notification channel. Verify state by asking.

steps.prompt: The service marks the order PAID and then publishes OrderPaid so shipping can start, but it crashes between the two steps. Which pattern removes that gap?
steps.context_note: The service updates its own database and then publishes to a message bus, and those are two separate writes.

options.text: Publish the event first, then update the database
Write the PAID update and the event to an outbox table in one transaction
Publish inside the database transaction block, just before it commits
Retry the publish a few times and log a warning if every attempt still fails

steps.explanation: Writing the state change and the event record in one database transaction removes the crash window, and a relay publishes outbox rows until they succeed, so consumers must handle duplicates. Publishing first only reverses the gap, and publishing before commit or retrying still leaves two independent writes.
steps.bottleneck_note: Never rely on two independent writes (database and message bus) staying in sync.

steps.prompt: A payment succeeds, but inventory now says the item just sold out and the money has already been taken. What should happen?
steps.context_note: The flow spans services, so no single database transaction can undo it.

options.text: Refund automatically and idempotently, and notify the customer
Hold the money as store credit without telling the customer
Roll back the payment and the inventory check together in one distributed transaction
Accept the order anyway and restock before dispatch

steps.explanation: Across services each step needs its own compensating action, so the order is cancelled with an automatic refund that is itself idempotent, plus a message to the customer. A distributed rollback across a bank and an inventory service is not available, and overselling or quietly holding money breaks trust and may breach regulations.
steps.bottleneck_note: If you cannot roll back, you must design the roll-forward undo.
